# The Final Step

> "Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free, and don't be entangled again with a yoke of bondage."
>
> — Galatians 5:1

You've settled the timing. You're ready for the final step.

It is not a final session. Chapter 1 promised you there would be no "one last time", and there isn't. Nobody sins once more for old times' sake on his way out of a sin. And you don't need to. Whenever your last time was, it's behind you now. You didn't mark it with a ceremony, and that's the right send-off for a thing that was never worth anything.

The final step is a decision, spoken out loud. For a believer it is a prayer, and for a man who doesn't pray there is a version right after it. Before you take it, check the two essentials.

1. **Are you certain?**
2. **Are you excited?** Do you have a sense of doom and gloom, or the feeling of a man about to do something marvelous?

If you have doubts on either count, stop here and re-read the book first. There's no hurry and no shame in it.

Nobody *decides* to fall into this trap. You wandered in as a boy. But the trap is built to hold you for life, and nobody wanders out of it. Getting out takes one clear, positive decision, and you're about to make it.

## "But I've promised this before" {-}

Of course you have, and you broke it every time. You may be afraid of breaking another.

Look at what you were promising then. You promised to go without something you still wanted. That was a vow against yourself, and half of you never signed it. Today is different, because there's nothing left that you want from it. You're only putting into words what has already happened in your head.

So don't think about failing. This time you aren't climbing by willpower. You're walking out through an open door, and you can enjoy the walk. If you're a Christian, you also have something stronger than your own word to stand on. A Christian counselor wrote it about pornography, and it holds for every form lust takes: "Jesus' grace to change you is stronger than pornography's power to destroy you."

And if what holds you back is the feeling that you've failed too often to come back again, hear a man who felt exactly that. He pictures the prodigal son, the runaway from the Introduction, halfway home, protesting that he still smells of the pigsty, and the Father answering with two words. "But God, I still smell like yesterday. Just come." He adds, for every man reading: "You're not too dirty. You're not too far."

A word about vows. Chapter 1 ruled out the willpower vow, and this isn't one. Jesus asked for plain speech: "But let your 'Yes' be 'Yes' and your 'No' be 'No.'" That is all this is: a plain No that you mean.

## If there is another person {-}

One thing comes before the prayer. If lust has you in an affair, paying for sex, or stringing a woman along, the decision you're about to make includes her. End it today. Don't end it with one last night. If you have deceived a wife or a partner, she is owed the truth, and Chapter 29 says how to tell her. If you've put her health at risk, get tested, and tell her that too. Being free is not the same as being trusted. Trust comes back slowly, and on her timetable.

## The prayer {-}

Here are the instructions.

**1. Go somewhere you can be alone and speak out loud.** Kneel if you're able. A man's body teaches his mind what's going on.

**2. Pray this.** Use your own words if you prefer, but don't make it long or clever.

> Father, I confess it.
>
> I have used my body, my eyes and my mind for lust. I have looked at women as things to use. I have done it in secret, told myself it was nothing, and hidden it from the people who love me. It was sin, and I am sorry.
>
> Forgive me, as you promised you would. Make me clean.
>
> Today I am finished with it. I am done with masturbation. I am done with porn. I am done with using a woman, or letting lust decide what I do about one. I will not feed lust with my eyes or my imagination. Whether I find it easy or hard, my answer is No.
>
> I can't keep this by my own strength, and I'm not going to try. Keep me. Make me a man who can be trusted, and make me fit for whatever you made me for. Then show me the man I am to go back for.
>
> Thank you that I am forgiven. Thank you that I am free.
>
> In Jesus's name. Amen.

**3. If you don't pray, say this instead.** Say it out loud, on your feet, to the man you intend to be. If you hold another faith, say it to God in the words your own faith gives you.

> I admit it.
>
> Lust has been making my decisions. It has cost me time, sleep, money and self-respect. I kept it secret, told myself it was nothing, and hid it from the people who love me. I have used people, on a screen and off it. That was wrong, and I am sorry.
>
> Today I am finished with it. I am done with masturbation. I am done with porn. I am done with using anyone, and with letting lust decide what I do. I will not feed it with my eyes or my imagination. Whether I find it easy or hard, my answer is No.
>
> I won't do this by gritting my teeth. I'll do it by remembering what I now know: it gave me nothing.
>
> I will be a man who can be trusted, and fit for the people and the work that are mine. And I will go back for one man who is still where I was.
>
> I am free.

Change the words until they are true of you. Name what it cost you. The sentence that matters is the plain No.

That is the whole of the final step. As a decision, it counts in full. A decision you've only thought is easy to un-think. One you've spoken has been heard, if only by you. If one day you want to pray the other version, it will still be here.

If you're Catholic, take this to Confession as well, and soon. The Church asks Catholics to bring sins like this to a priest. Many men say that was the moment the weight came off. Your priest has heard it all before, and he is bound never to repeat a word of it.

**4. Then stand up and say it:**

**"YES! I'M FREE!"**

Shout it if the neighbors can stand it.

Don't get up thinking "I must never do that again" or "I'm not allowed anymore". Those are a prisoner's sentences. Get up thinking, "Isn't it wonderful? I never have to do that again. I'm free."

Do it now.

## The first three days {-}

Chapter 22 covers the first weeks. If you were at it every day, here is a plain plan for the first seventy-two hours. None of it is willpower. It is only good sense.

- **Tonight, clear the way.** Charge the phone outside the bedroom. Delete the folder, the app and her number.
- **Know your hour.** You know when the bell usually rings: the shower, the empty house, midnight. Expect it. A bell you saw coming is only a bell.
- **When the urge comes, do nothing.** Don't argue with it and don't obey it. It fades in a minute or two. Say "I'm free", and carry on with what you were doing.
- **Eat, sleep and get outside.** A tired, hungry man alone indoors feels everything worse than it is.
- **If you lie awake, lie there and be glad.** It is two or three nights at most, and you know what is dying.
- **Tell one person you trust** before the three days are up. A friend, a brother, a pastor, a counselor or a doctor will do. Chapter 29 says how.
- **If you fall,** read If You Slip the same hour, and refuse the second one.

By the end of three days you'll have met most of your cues once and let them ring. The rest is the same, only easier.

## Let it ring {-}

A surgeon turned writer named Maxwell Maltz had a picture for this, and it's worth carrying with you.

Imagine you're sitting in an armchair and the telephone rings. All your life you've jumped up to answer it. Today you stay in the chair. You can hear it perfectly well. You're not pretending it isn't ringing, and you're not gripping the armrests. You just don't get up.

Two things follow. First, the ringing has no power of its own. A bell is a noise in the air and can't lift a man out of a chair. It only ever moved you because you'd formed the habit of obeying it. Second, not answering takes no effort. You aren't wrestling the phone. You're doing nothing at all, and doing it comfortably.

Every cue you'll meet is that telephone. It may be the empty house, the photo in the feed, the bed at midnight, the bad day or the message from her. Let it ring. It will stop.

## You are already free {-}

Only two things can make this hard: doubting and waiting. So never doubt the decision. You know it's right. If you start to question it, you put yourself where you can't win. You'll be miserable if you don't, and worse if you do.

Ask what you're actually trying to achieve. It isn't simply "never to do any of it again". Plenty of men manage that and feel robbed until they die. Think instead about the man who has never had the habit. He isn't different from you because he resists. He doesn't want it. He has no craving, and he isn't using any willpower.

That's what you're after, and it's within reach. You don't have to wait to become that man. You started being him when you said it, and God finishes what he starts.

You are already a free man.

On good days and bad, don't build your life around having stopped. If you do, you'll turn something that cost you nothing into a real sacrifice. You haven't given up living. You've been healed of something and let out of somewhere. The weeks will go by, and your energy and your conscience will recover. Your good days will be better and your bad days milder than they ever were.

And whenever the thought of it crosses your mind, tomorrow or in forty years, be glad. You're free.

## A final warning {-}

Men who have walked out and lived happily for years do go back in. I hope this book has made stopping easy for you. But a man who finds stopping easy can find starting again just as easy.

**Don't fall for that.**

However long you've been free, and however sure you are that you could never be caught again, keep one lifelong rule: not once, for any reason. A lonely anniversary doesn't count as a reason. Neither does "to help me sleep", or "just to see". The old inclination is asleep. Don't wake it.

The rule is strict, and the grace is real. If you ever do fall, a short chapter called If You Slip tells you what to do. Don't plan on needing it.

Remember what that one time would do for you. It would do nothing. You'd have no itch for it to relieve, and you'd feel foolish and flat. But it would wake the Little Monster, and a small voice in your head would say, "Another." Then you'd have two choices. You could be miserable for a while as he starves again, or you could start the whole dreary chain from the beginning.

Paul wrote his sentence to people who were already free. He didn't tell them to try to get free. He told them to stand firm in it, and not to be "entangled again".

You're free, so stand firm.
